title: Smoky Jollof Rice with Charred Pepper Relish
excerpt: The one-pot rice that anchors a Nigerian table — cooked low, finished with fire, and brightened with a fresh pepper relish.
imageAlt: Jollof rice with grilled chicken and roasted vegetables on a serving dish
body:
Jollof is not a recipe so much as an argument — about smoke, about patience, and about whose grandmother did it best. I am not here to settle that argument. I am here to teach you the version I cook in professional kitchens: deep red, gently smoky, every grain separate, and genuinely good for you when you build the plate around it.

The two things that change everything are the base and the heat control. The base is not a sauce you pour on at the end; it is the flavour foundation that the rice absorbs as it cooks. And the heat must stay low — a hard boil will give you rice that is cooked on the outside and chalky in the middle.

## My nutrition note

Jollof often gets treated as a carbohydrate to work around. I like to flip that. Cook it with brown or parboiled rice, add a handful of peas or chopped greens in the last ten minutes, and serve it with a generous portion of grilled fish or chicken. You get fibre, protein, resistant starch and a plate that does not feel like a compromise.

## Make it ahead

The base can be blended and cooked down two days ahead — it actually improves overnight. Keep it in the fridge and bring it to room temperature before adding the rice.
ingredients: 400 g long-grain parboiled or brown rice, rinsed until the water runs clear
2 red bell peppers, deseeded and chopped
1 large scotch bonnet (adjust to your heat), stemmed
1 large onion, half blended and half finely sliced
1 litre good vegetable or chicken stock, hot
1 tsp fine sea salt, or to taste
2 handfuls frozen peas or chopped spinach, to finish
For the relish: 1 red onion, 1 red pepper, 1 chilli, juice of 1 lime, small bunch of coriander
steps: Blend the tomatoes, red peppers, scotch bonnet and the roughly chopped half of the onion until smooth. Set aside.
Warm the oil in a heavy-bottomed pot over a medium heat. Add the sliced onion with a pinch of salt and cook for 5 minutes until soft and just gold at the edges.
Stir in the tomato paste and cook it out for 3 minutes — it should darken to brick red and smell sweet rather than sharp.

Pour in the blended pepper base. Add the smoked paprika, thyme, curry powder and bay leaves. Simmer uncovered for 20 to 25 minutes, stirring often, until the sauce has reduced by almost half and the oil begins to sit on top.

Stir the rinsed rice through the base so every grain is coated. Toast it in the pot for 3 minutes, then pour in the hot stock. Season with salt, bring to a bare simmer, cover tightly and reduce the heat to the lowest setting.

Cook for 25 to 30 minutes without stirring. At the 20-minute mark, scatter the peas or spinach over the top, replace the lid and let them steam through. If the rice is still firm, add a splash of hot water and give it 5 more minutes.
Kill the heat and let the pot rest, lid on, for 10 minutes. Fork through gently, then taste — jollof almost always needs one more pinch of salt than you expect.
For the relish, finely dice the onion, pepper and chilli, toss with lime juice, salt and torn coriander, and spoon over the rice at the table.

title: Berbere-Roasted Fish with Citrus Herb Salad
excerpt: A whole fish rubbed in berbere and olive oil, roasted hot and fast, then laid over a sharp citrus salad. Twenty minutes of work, one memorable table.
imageAlt: Whole roasted fish with herbs, lemon and vegetables on a plate
body:
This is the dish I cook when I want people to stop talking and start eating. It is built from two ideas: the deep, warm heat of berbere against the clean acidity of citrus, and a hot oven that respects the fish enough to leave it alone.

Ask your fishmonger to clean and score the fish, and to scale it if the skin is heavy. Scoring matters — it lets the spice paste reach the flesh and helps a thick fish cook evenly. I keep the head on because it protects the moisture and because it looks like dinner, not a fillet.

## On the berbere

Berbere varies wildly from kitchen to kitchen. Taste yours first. If it is very hot, use less and add more paprika. If it is heavy on fenugreek or cardamom, a little honey in the paste will round it out. There is no shame in buying a blend you trust.

## Serving

The salad below is deliberately sharp. With grilled flatbread, roasted sweet potato or a spoon of cool yoghurt, this is a complete plate — protein, greens, healthy fat and acid, all in balance.
ingredients: 1 whole sea bass or bream, about 1.2 kg, cleaned and scored
1 lemon, half juiced and half sliced
For the salad: 2 oranges, peeled and sliced into rounds
1 small red onion, very thinly sliced
1 handful each flat-leaf parsley and mint
steps: Heat the oven to 220°C (200°C fan). Line a large tray with baking paper.
Mix the berbere, olive oil, garlic, honey, salt and lemon juice into a loose paste.
Pat the fish dry inside and out. Rub the paste all over, working it into the scored flesh and the cavity. Stuff the cavity with the lemon slices.
Roast for 18 to 22 minutes, until the skin is crisp and the flesh at the thickest point flakes away from the bone. Let it rest for 5 minutes — no shortcuts here.
While the fish roasts, soak the sliced onion in cold water for 5 minutes, then drain. Toss with the orange, fennel, herbs, olive oil, lemon juice and cumin. Season lightly.
Lay the fish on a platter, spoon the salad and its juices around it, and finish with a final drizzle of olive oil and cracked pepper.

title: Misir Wot & Gomen with Teff Injera
excerpt: Two of Ethiopia's most generous plant-based stews, cooked side by side and scooped up with sour, spongy teff injera.
imageAlt: A generous platter of African stews, rice and vegetables served on a wooden tray
body:
The Ethiopian table taught me that plant-based eating does not need a label or a compromise. A fasting platter — served on injera, eaten with your hands — is one of the most complete, most joyful meals I know.

Misir wot is red lentils cooked down with berbere and onion until they are almost jammy. Gomen is collard greens, slow and soft, with ginger and garlic. Together they cover protein, iron, fibre and a serious amount of flavour, with no meat on the table.

## About the injera

Traditional injera needs a teff starter and two to three days of fermentation. If you have a reliable Ethiopian bakery nearby, buy it — good injera is a craft. If you want to make it at home, start with a 100% teff flour batter, keep it somewhere warm, and be patient. The sourness you are looking for is time, not vinegar.

## Make it a platter

Serve with a spoon of cool ayib or yoghurt, a handful of raw onion and green chilli, and a simple beet salad. The point is contrast: hot and cool, soft and sharp, red and green.
ingredients: For the misir wot: 250 g red lentils, rinsed
3 tbsp niter kibbeh or olive oil
1.2 litres hot water or vegetable stock
For the gomen: 500 g collard greens, stems removed and shredded
2 tbsp niter kibbeh or olive oil
To serve: 6 teff injera, yoghurt, sliced raw onion, green chilli and lemon
steps: Start the wot. Cook the onion in a dry pot over a medium heat for 5 minutes, then add the fat and a pinch of salt. Cook for another 5 minutes until translucent — dry-cooking the onion first builds sweetness without extra oil.
Add the garlic, ginger and tomato paste and stir for 2 minutes. Add the berbere and cook for 1 minute more, stirring constantly so it does not catch.

Tip in the lentils and hot water. Simmer, partially covered, for 25 to 30 minutes, stirring now and then, until the lentils have collapsed into a thick stew. Top up with hot water if it gets too tight. Season with salt.
For the gomen, warm the fat in a wide pan and soften the onion for 6 minutes. Add the garlic, ginger, cardamom and chilli and stir for 1 minute.
Add the collards in handfuls, tossing as they wilt. Add a splash of water, cover and cook gently for 15 to 20 minutes until tender and glossy. Season well.
Spread the injera over a large platter, spoon the misir wot and gomen on top, and add yoghurt, raw onion, chilli and lemon at the edges. Eat with your right hand, folding as you go.

title: Suya-Spiced Chicken & Fonio Grain Bowl
excerpt: Yaji spice, charred chicken and ancient West African fonio — the lunch bowl I make on repeat, built for energy rather than heaviness.
imageAlt: A colourful grain bowl with grilled chicken, quinoa, vegetables and seeds
body:
Fonio is one of the oldest grains in West Africa and one of the fastest to cook — three minutes, if you treat it kindly. It has a delicate, nutty flavour, a low glycaemic index and more than enough personality to carry a spice-heavy bowl like this one.

Suya spice, or yaji, is the point of the whole plate: groundnut, chilli, ginger, garlic, paprika and a warm hum of clove and cinnamon. I use it twice — once as a marinade and once as a finishing dust so the flavour stays bright.

## The build

A good grain bowl needs five things: a grain, a protein, something raw and crunchy, something creamy, and acid. Miss one and the bowl feels flat. Here the acid comes from quick-pickled onions, the creaminess from a yoghurt-tahini drizzle, and the crunch from cabbage and toasted peanuts.
ingredients: 3 tbsp suya spice (yaji), plus extra to finish
200 g fonio, rinsed (or use bulgur or quinoa)
1 small red onion, thinly sliced and pickled in lime juice
Small handful each mint and coriander
steps: Mix the suya spice, oil, tomato paste, lime juice and salt into a paste. Coat the chicken and leave it for at least 20 minutes — overnight in the fridge is better.

Bring the water to a boil in a small pan, add a pinch of salt and stir in the rinsed fonio. Cover, turn the heat to its lowest and steam for 3 minutes. Take it off the heat and leave it covered for 5 minutes, then fluff with a fork.
Heat a heavy griddle or frying pan until it is properly hot. Cook the chicken for 5 to 6 minutes a side, until charred in patches and cooked through. Rest for 5 minutes, then slice.
Stir the yoghurt and tahini together with a pinch of salt and a splash of water until it is pourable.
Build the bowls: fonio first, then cabbage, carrot, pickled onion and sliced chicken. Spoon over the yoghurt drizzle.
Finish with the herbs, crushed peanuts and a final dusting of suya spice. Serve with lime wedges.

title: Market Greens with Tamarind & Toasted Peanut
excerpt: A five-minute salad that behaves like a proper dish: bitter leaves, sweet tomato, sour tamarind and a salty peanut crunch.
imageAlt: A fresh platter of sliced cucumbers, tomatoes, onions and lemons
body:
I have a rule in my kitchen: if a salad cannot stand on its own at the table, it does not belong on the menu. This one does. It is the plate I bring to every gathering because it takes minutes and makes people ask for the recipe.

Tamarind is the engine. Soak a block of it in hot water, push it through a sieve, and you have a sour, fruity concentrate that works like a more interesting lemon. Mixed with honey, oil and a little fish sauce or soy, it becomes a dressing that can carry stronger leaves.

## Use what is good

Swap the greens for whatever is crisp and local. The technique matters more than the ingredient list: bitter, sweet, sour, salty and fat, all in one bowl. Taste, adjust, taste again.
ingredients: 40 g tamarind block, soaked in 100 ml hot water and strained
1 tsp soy sauce or fish sauce
200 g mixed greens: rocket, spinach, watercress or young kale
Small handful mint and coriander leaves
steps: Whisk the strained tamarind, honey, oil, soy, chilli and ginger until it is glossy. It should taste aggressively sour and a little sweet — it will soften once it hits the leaves.
Soak the sliced onion in iced water for 5 minutes and drain well. This takes away the raw sting and keeps the crunch.
In a wide bowl, layer the greens, tomatoes, cucumber and onion.
Spoon over the dressing just before serving and toss lightly with your hands so nothing is bruised.
Finish with crushed peanuts, mint and coriander. Serve immediately.

title: Hibiscus, Mango & Coconut Chia Parfait
excerpt: Zobo hibiscus syrup, coconut chia and ripe mango in a glass — a dessert that is quietly full of fibre and entirely worth a second spoon.
imageAlt: Close-up of a chef garnishing a layered chocolate and fruit dessert
body:
Hibiscus is the ingredient my kitchen never runs out of. In West Africa we drink it as zobo, cooled and spiced with ginger and cloves. Here I reduce the same drink into a syrup and use it twice — in the cream and as a ruby drizzle over the top.

This is a dessert built on contrast: creamy coconut, tart hibiscus, sweet mango and the gentle pop of chia. It needs to be made ahead, which is exactly what you want in a dessert.

## Sober about sweetness

I use only as much sugar as the fruit needs. A ripe mango is already dessert. If yours is underripe, let the fruit sit for a day with the lime juice and a teaspoon of sugar before you assemble.
ingredients: 2 tbsp honey or light brown sugar
400 ml coconut milk (or a 60/40 mix with yoghurt)
2 ripe mangoes, half blended into a puree and half diced
steps: Simmer the hibiscus, water, honey, cloves and ginger for 10 minutes, then strain. Reduce the liquid to about 120 ml so it is syrupy. Cool completely.
Stir the chia into the coconut milk with the vanilla and 2 tablespoons of the hibiscus syrup. Leave for 15 minutes, stir again to break up any clumps, then chill for at least 2 hours or overnight.
Toss the diced mango with lime juice and zest.
Build four glasses: a spoon of mango puree, a layer of chia, the diced mango, then another layer of chia.
Finish with hibiscus syrup, toasted coconut, lime zest and mint. Serve cold.

title: The pantry I travel with: seven ingredients, six countries
excerpt: A chef's suitcase says a lot about her. Mine is mostly berbere, dried shrimp and a very serious bag of peppercorns.
imageAlt: Colourful spices displayed in sacks at a market with yellow and red mounds
body:
I have packed a kitchen into a suitcase more times than I can count. Doha to Bermuda. Nassau to New York. Addis to wherever the next kitchen is. You learn quickly that you cannot take everything, and that the things you insist on carrying are the things that tell you who you are.

Here is what is always in my bag, and what each one is really for.

## Berbere

Not just heat. Berbere is a whole argument about balance — chilli, fenugreek, cardamom, clove, ginger, ajwain. A spoon of it can turn onions, lentils and oil into something with depth. I buy it from a spice stall I trust in Addis and wrap it twice.

## Dried shrimp

A small handful, fried in oil, gives a bowl of greens or rice a savoury backbone that no stock cube can match. This is the ingredient I use when I want a vegetable dish to taste big.

## Grains of selim

Peppery, floral, a little smoky. I add them to braises and to tea. In West Africa they appear where black pepper might, and once you have cooked with them, ordinary pepper feels a bit one-dimensional.

## Tamarind

Acid is the thing most home cooks under-season. Tamarind gives sourness with a fruitiness that lemon cannot. A block of it lasts months and transforms a salad dressing in a minute.

## Palm oil

Genuinely irreplaceable. That red colour and grassy, almost smoky perfume is the taste of a whole cooking tradition. It is also rich in vitamin A and in the polyphenols that make it a subject of serious nutrition research. Use it with respect and good heat.

## Dried hibiscus

Cheap, light and generous. Infuse it for drinks, reduce it for syrup, or grind it into a rub for fish. It is the reason I can always produce a dessert from almost nothing.

## A jar of my mother's pepper base

Blended onion, pepper and tomato, cooked down until it is almost concentrated. I have not travelled without it in twelve years. It is partly practical — a base ready in minutes — and partly the point of this entire list. Technique travels. Memory travels with you only if you pack it.

## What this says about a pantry

The most important ingredient in any kitchen is not something rare. It is the thing you understand completely. Build a shelf of seven ingredients you know intimately, and you can feed people anywhere in the world.

title: Cooking with Marcus Samuelsson at Marcus Addis
excerpt: In Addis Ababa, Odi and Marcus Samuelsson bring Ethiopian ingredients into new forms. Their hand-cut teff tagliatelle tells that story.
imageAlt: Chef Odi and Marcus Samuelsson working together at the counter in the Marcus Addis kitchen
body:
Odi has worked alongside Marcus Samuelsson since 2017. At Marcus Addis, the collaboration starts with ingredients that already matter to the people who eat them. What changes is the technique, or the way those ingredients meet on a plate.

## Teff takes a different shape

In its profile of Marcus Addis, Bon Appétit describes Odi and Marcus working through dough ratios for a hand-cut teff tagliatelle. It arrives with roasted tomato Bolognese, spinach, lemon zest and Parmesan. A grain best known in Ethiopia for injera gets another form without losing its distinct flavour.

## Behind the pass

The kitchen photographs shared on @chefodigowa show that work in progress: cooks tasting together, working the pass and trying ideas before they make it to the dining room.

title: Why African cuisines belong in the nutrition conversation
excerpt: Millet, fonio, cowpeas, leafy greens, fermented grains: the most useful nutrition advice in the world may already be in your grandmother's kitchen.
imageAlt: A vibrant spread of fresh vegetables and herbs for healthy cooking
body:
Nutrition conversations have a habit of arriving in African countries as a correction. Eat less of this, replace that, try this imported alternative. I have sat in too many rooms where the local food was treated as the problem rather than the starting point.

The evidence keeps pointing somewhere else. Many traditional African diets are built on exactly what the research recommends: a wide variety of plants, whole grains, legumes, fermented foods and small amounts of animal protein used as seasoning rather than the centre of the plate.

## What is actually on the plate

Consider a simple West African meal of beans, plantain and greens. Fibre from the beans, resistant starch, potassium, vitamin A and iron from the greens, a good hit of plant protein — and a fraction of the cost of the imported wellness shelf. Or an Ethiopian platter of lentils, collards and teff injera: iron, calcium, protein and probiotics from the fermentation.

This is not a niche observation. It is a serious public health opportunity, and it is being under-used.

## The barriers are real

I am not romantic about this. Urban diets are shaped by price, time and marketing. Indigenous grains are often harder to buy, and in some places more expensive than imported rice. A nutrition advocate who ignores that is not much use. So my work sits in three places: recipe development that makes these ingredients convenient, sourcing conversations with producers, and storytelling that makes the food desirable rather than dutiful.

## Three things I would change

First, teach the local pantry in nutrition education, not the imported one. Second, invest in processing and distribution for indigenous grains so they can compete on time and price. Third, give African chefs and home cooks a seat at the policy table — we know what people will actually eat.

Flavour is not the enemy of nutrition. It is the delivery mechanism.

title: A café table in Addis: notes on coffee, patience and community
excerpt: The coffee ceremony is not a coffee break. It is a reminder that a table can hold an entire day — and that I should design menus the same way.
imageAlt: A cup of coffee and lush green leaves on a wooden café table
body:
There is a café in Addis where I go to write. Green plastic chairs, a hand-painted wall, and a buna ceremony that starts when the owner decides it should. Nobody hurries it. The beans are roasted in front of you, the incense curls over the cups, and the first pour goes to whoever is sitting closest.

I have spent twenty years learning efficiency in professional kitchens. This is the opposite lesson, and I need it.

## The ceremony as a menu lesson

Three pours, three rounds of conversation. The strength changes each time — the first is the boldest, the last almost tea-like. It is a beautifully considered sequence that respects both the ingredient and the guest.

I want my menus to behave like that. Not fourteen dishes competing for attention, but a sequence with a beginning, a deepening, and an unhurried ending. A plate of pickles at the start. A main that comes with bread and time. Something small and sweet at the end, with tea.

## What I wrote in my notebook

Hospitality is a pace, not just a welcome. A room can be designed to slow people down.

If a café can make me a regular in four visits, it is not because of the coffee alone. It is because a person at that table noticed me. That is the part of the experience no software can design.

## Back in my kitchen

Since that trip I have stopped padding menus with choices. I cook fewer dishes, better, and I leave more room for the table to do its work. It is a small change with a long history behind it.

The next time you are in Addis, order the coffee and stay for all three rounds. You will learn more about hospitality than any course can teach you.

title: Ethiopian Kinche: Cracked Barley Porridge
excerpt: A simple Ethiopian breakfast made with cracked barley and finished with onion, green chilli and coriander. Adapted from Odi’s recipe for the Chefs’ Manifesto.
imageAlt: A bowl of cracked-barley kinche with green chilli and coriander
body:
Kinche is a traditional Ethiopian breakfast made with cracked grain. The barley cooks gently until tender. Fresh onion, green chilli, coriander and a little olive oil are all it needs at the table.

## About this version

This home-kitchen version is adapted from Chef Odi’s kinche recipe for the Chefs’ Manifesto. It keeps the cracked barley and savoury finish, with optional toppings to make it a fuller breakfast.
ingredients: 1 tbsp olive oil, plus extra to finish
Optional: 100 g cooked chickpeas, or a soft-boiled egg per bowl
steps: Bring the water to a boil in a heavy pot.
Add the cracked barley and the salt and stir well.
Lower the heat, cover and simmer for 15 to 20 minutes, until the grains have absorbed the water and are tender. Stir occasionally so the bottom does not catch.
Taste and adjust the salt. If the porridge is too thick, loosen it with a splash of hot water — it should be spoonable, not stiff.
Divide between warm bowls and finish with olive oil, diced onion, green chilli and coriander.
Add chickpeas, egg or toasted seeds if you want a more substantial plate. Serve immediately.

title: Teff & Sorghum Croquettes with Greens
excerpt: Crisp croquettes made with teff, sorghum and millet over a spinach sauce, inspired by Chef Odi’s Culinary Village demonstration.
imageAlt: A colourful grain bowl with grilled vegetables and fresh greens
body:
At the Culinary Village in Kigali, Odi cooked croquettes made from sorghum, millet and teff, served with isombe. This home-kitchen adaptation uses spinach in its sauce, rather than the cassava leaves used in the original dish.

## Make it ahead

Cook the grains until tender, mix them with mashed beans and chill the mixture completely before shaping. Fry the croquettes just before serving and spoon them over warm greens.
ingredients: 200 g cooked white beans, mashed (or 1 large potato, mashed)
For the greens: 300 g spinach, finely chopped
2 tbsp palm oil or olive oil
steps: Simmer the sorghum in 300 ml of the water for 35 to 40 minutes until tender, then drain well. Cook the teff and millet together in the remaining water for 15 minutes, then rest off the heat for 5 minutes.

Combine all three grains with the salt, mashed beans, paprika, ginger and spring onions. Mix firmly — you want a cohesive, slightly sticky dough. Cool completely in the fridge for at least 30 minutes.
For the sauce, warm the oil and soften the onion for 6 minutes. Add the garlic and chilli. Stir in the spinach and cook until wilted and tender. Stir in the ground peanuts, season and keep warm.
Shape the chilled grain mix into 12 small croquettes. Roll them lightly between your palms so they hold together.
Heat 3 cm of oil to 170°C. Fry the croquettes in small batches for 3 to 4 minutes, until deep gold and crisp. Drain on a rack, never on paper, so they stay crisp.
Spoon the greens onto plates, sit the croquettes on top, and finish with ground peanuts and coriander.

title: Whole Roasted Cauliflower with Spiced Butter
excerpt: A whole roast cauliflower glazed in spiced butter and finished with peanuts, inspired by Chef Odi’s post about bringing out the best in the vegetable.
imageAlt: Whole roasted cauliflower glazed with spiced butter, peanuts, pomegranate and herb sauce
body:
This recipe takes its cue from a post by Chef Odi on how good cauliflower can be with a chef’s touch. It’s a home-kitchen interpretation, not a transcription of his dish.

The technique is simple but needs patience. Simmer the whole head first so the inside cooks evenly, then roast it until the outside goes golden and crisp at the tips. Spiced butter does the rest.

## Serving

Serve it as a vegetarian main with a grain salad or as a side with grilled fish. Peanuts bring crunch, while pomegranate and lemon give the roasted cauliflower a bright finish.
ingredients: 1 whole cauliflower, about 900 g, leaves trimmed
For the herb sauce: 1 handful parsley, 1 handful coriander, 1 green chilli, 1 garlic clove, 4 tbsp olive oil, juice of half a lemon, pinch of salt
steps: Heat the oven to 200°C (180°C fan). Bring a large pot of salted water to a boil.
Lower the whole cauliflower into the water and simmer for 6 to 8 minutes, until a knife slides into the core with a little resistance. Drain well and let it steam dry for 5 minutes.
Warm the butter with the berbere, garlic, honey, salt and lemon juice for 1 minute so the spices bloom. Do not let the garlic brown.
Set the cauliflower in a roasting tin and spoon over the spiced butter, working it into the florets. Roast for 35 to 45 minutes, basting twice, until deep gold and crisp at the edges.
Blitz the herb sauce ingredients to a loose green sauce. Taste and adjust the lemon and salt.
Spoon the herb sauce onto a plate, sit the cauliflower on top and finish with crushed peanuts, pomegranate seeds and coriander.

title: Millet Porridge with Cinnamon, Star Anise & Turmeric
excerpt: Finger millet with cinnamon, star anise and turmeric. A home-kitchen take on Chef Arabella Parkinson’s Culinary Village porridge, finished with fruit and toasted seeds.
imageAlt: A warm bowl of millet porridge topped with fruit, seeds and warming spices
body:
At the Culinary Village in Kigali, Chef Arabella Parkinson served warm millet porridge scented with cinnamon, star anise and turmeric. This home-kitchen version uses the same spice combination to bring out the nuttiness of the grain.

## Make it yours

Finger or pearl millet can both work here. Adjust the liquid for the texture you like and finish with seasonal fruit, yoghurt or toasted pumpkin seeds. Take out the whole spices before serving.
ingredients: 150 g finger millet (or pearl millet), rinsed and soaked 30 minutes
500 ml water, plus extra as needed
1 tbsp honey or brown sugar, to taste
To serve: sliced banana or mango, thick yoghurt, toasted pumpkin seeds, ground cinnamon
steps: Drain the millet. Warm a heavy pot over a medium heat and toast the cinnamon stick, star anise and turmeric for 30 seconds, until fragrant.
Add the millet and stir for 1 minute so it picks up the spices.
Pour in the water and salt. Bring to a simmer, cover and cook for 15 minutes, stirring occasionally.
Add the milk, honey and vanilla. Simmer uncovered for 8 to 10 minutes, stirring, until the porridge is thick and creamy. Add hot water if it tightens too much.
Remove the cinnamon and star anise. Taste and adjust the sweetness.
Spoon into bowls and top with fruit, yoghurt, pumpkin seeds and a little extra cinnamon.
